lit.'<p>Desde la Revolución Industrial la qu:
'

Since the Industrial Revolution, burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised CO₂ from 280 ppm to over 420 ppm, as the Mauna Loa measurements show (the Keeling curve). More CO₂ means a radiative forcing ΔF = 5.35·ln(C/280) W/m², and global temperature has already risen ≈ 1.2 °C. The data in the graph are real measurements.

'
lit.'<p>El <b>tiempo atmosférico</b> es el e:
'

Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given moment (it is raining today); climate is the average over decades in a place. Climate is a dynamic system: the atmosphere, hydrosphere (oceans), cryosphere (ice), geosphere and biosphere exchange energy, water and carbon, and a change in one part affects the others.

'
lit.'<p>El hielo y la nieve reflejan mucha l:
'

Ice and snow reflect a lot of light (high albedo); oceans and forests reflect little. If the Earth warms, ice melts, the surface darkens and absorbs more energy: it warms even more. This is a positive feedback, which amplifies changes. Water vapour gives another: warmer air holds more vapour, which is a greenhouse gas.

'
lit.'<p>El vapor de agua, el CO₂, el metano:
'

Water vapour, CO₂, methane and other greenhouse gases absorb part of the infrared emitted by the surface and re-emit it in all directions, including downwards. This raises the mean temperature from −18 °C to ≈ 15 °C. This natural greenhouse effect makes life as we know it possible.

'
lit.'<p>La Tierra recibe <b>luz solar</b> (≈:
'

The Earth receives sunlight (≈ 1361 W/m² outside the atmosphere) and reflects ≈ 30 % (the albedo). The rest warms it and it emits infrared radiation. At equilibrium, the energy coming in equals the energy going out. Without an atmosphere, that balance would give a mean temperature of ≈ −18 °C.

'
lit.'<p>Si el CO₂ llegara a 560 ppm (el dobl:
'

If CO₂ reached 560 ppm (double the pre-industrial level), the model predicts ≈ 3 °C more. Consequences: heatwaves, droughts (central Chile has been in a megadrought since 2010), retreating glaciers, sea-level rise and loss of biodiversity. Mitigation (renewable energy, efficiency, clean transport, protecting forests) and adaptation reduce the risks.

'
